tagline: The studio standard, largely because tethering actually works.
verdictSummary: Capture One is bought by studio photographers for one reason more than any other: a camera plugged into a laptop appears, fires, and drops full-resolution files into a session, reliably, for over five hundred camera models. Each of those is a proprietary protocol reverse-engineered and maintained through firmware changes. That long tail is not a codebase you write, it is a decade of unglamorous compatibility work, and it settles the verdict.
coreLoopDIY: Run a tethered session using the manufacturer's own tools, and own the part around it: files landing in a dated session folder, backed up as they arrive, with a client-facing view that refreshes.
whatYouLose: tethering for hundreds of camera models, maintained through firmware updates
the colour profiles and raw conversion Capture One is known for
live view, focus control and camera settings from the laptop
the iPad application and the collaboration tools
sessions and catalogues designed around commercial studio work
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a tethering failure in front of a client and a paid crew costs more in ten minutes than the licence costs in a year, and reliability across every camera in the room is what the money buys.
prompt:
Build the session layer around a tethered shoot. The capture itself is done by your camera manufacturer's own tethering utility, and the README should say so plainly rather than pretending otherwise.

Stack: a local application, SQLite, no network required.

Session: created with a name, a date, a client and a shot list. It owns a folder with a fixed structure — captures, selects, exports — created on disk immediately so the shape exists before anything is shot.

Watch the capture folder. As each file lands:
1. Copy it to a second location you configure — a different physical disk — **before** anything else. In-camera cards get formatted at the end of the day; a single copy on one laptop is how a shoot gets lost. Show the copy status per file and refuse to mark a session complete while any file is unmirrored.
2. Extract the embedded preview and metadata, and add it to a live grid.
3. Match it to the current shot-list item, which you advance manually.

The client view is a separate full-screen window, intended for a second monitor: the latest capture large, with the last few as thumbnails, auto-advancing as files arrive, and nothing else on screen — no menus, no file names, no ratings. Photographers currently do this with a shared folder and a slideshow, badly.

Ratings and rejects from the keyboard, written to sidecars beside the originals.

End of session: a report of frames per shot-list item, flagging any item with no captures, which is the check worth running before the client leaves the building.

Export: a contact sheet as PDF, and a selects folder of full-resolution copies with a naming template.

Write tests for the mirror-before-index ordering, for the session refusing to complete with unmirrored files, and for shot-list matching across an advance.

Do not implement camera control or raw development.

faq.q: Why is tethering support such a long tail?
faq.a: Because every manufacturer has its own protocol, quirks per body, and firmware updates that change behaviour. Supporting five hundred cameras means owning or borrowing them and fixing them one at a time, forever. It is the least glamorous moat in this catalogue and one of the most solid.

faq.q: Why mirror files before indexing them?
faq.a: Because the window between "the card is full" and "the card is formatted" is where shoots are lost, and a laptop disk is one failure away from being the only copy. Ordering the mirror first makes the safety property real rather than best-effort.

faq.q: Is the client view really worth building?
faq.a: It is the feature working photographers improvise most often and worst. A clean second screen that just shows the last frame keeps a client engaged and stops them reading your file names and rejects over your shoulder.

faq.q: Can I leave Capture One with my work intact?
faq.a: Sessions are folders of raws with sidecars, so the files come with you. The adjustments are proprietary — styles, layers and colour edits do not translate to another developer — so treat a migration as re-developing the images you still care about.
